summary: This note is a wiki-style overview of the Hellenistic period, covering roughly 323 BCE (Alexander the Great's death) to 31 BCE (Battle of Actium and the Roman conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt). It describes political developments such as Rhodes' independence, the Ptolemaic and Seleucid kingdoms, the Roman wars with Macedon, and the Roman absorption of Greece and Macedon. It also covers ruler cults, the cultural and scientific achievements of the era, changes in art style, and the Hellenistic history of Judea leading to the Maccabean Revolt.
one_line: Overview of the Hellenistic period (323–31 BCE), covering the successor kingdoms, Roman conquest of Greece and Macedon, and Hellenistic culture and art.
key_facts: Rhodes maintained full independence from Hellenistic kingdoms and held out for one year under siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes (304-305 BCE).
The Rhodians built the Colossus of Rhodes to commemorate their victory over Demetrius Poliorcetes.
The Ptolemies in Egypt adopted earlier Pharaonic practice and established themselves as god-kings, with cults such as the Ptolemaieia at Alexandria.
The Hellenistic period covers the years between the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC and the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, followed by the conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt the following year.
Ptolemy's family ruled Egypt until the Roman conquest of 30 BC; the last ruler, Cleopatra VII, ended Ptolemaic rule with her suicide at the conquest by Rome.
The Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) saw Seleucus crush Antigonus, who was killed, while Lysimachus took Ionia, Seleucus took Cilicia, and Ptolemy captured Cyprus.
The Second Macedonian War ended with a decisive Roman victory at the Battle of Cynoscephalae (197 BC), followed by the 'Peace of Flaminius'.
Macedon was formally annexed as a Roman province in 146 BC after a rebellion under Andriscus.
The Roman consul Lucius Mummius defeated the Greeks at Corinth, which was razed to the ground, and in 146 BC the Greek peninsula became a Roman protectorate.
Alexandria and Antioch were the great centers of Hellenistic culture, capitals of Ptolemaic Egypt and Seleucid Syria respectively.
The Hellenistic period saw the rise of New Comedy, Alexandrian poetry, the Septuagint, and the philosophies of Stoicism and Epicureanism.
Greek science was advanced by the mathematician Euclid and the polymath Archimedes.
Hellenistic art shifted from idealistic classical figures toward realism and the depiction of emotion (pathos) and character (ethos).
Judea was ruled by the hereditary office of the High Priest as a Hellenistic vassal, and the Maccabean Revolt of Judas Maccabeus (174–135 BCE) is celebrated in the festival of Hanukkah.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes sacked Jerusalem and looted the Temple in 169 BCE after disturbances in Judea during his abortive invasion of Egypt.

entities.name: Rhodes
entities.role: city state that maintained full independence from Hellenistic kingdoms through a skilled navy and neutral posture

entities.name: Demetrius Poliorcetes
entities.role: besieged Rhodes for one year (304-305 BCE)

entities.name: Colossus of Rhodes
entities.role: monument built by the Rhodians to commemorate their victory over Demetrius Poliorcetes

entities.name: Ptolemies
entities.role: dynasty that ruled Egypt and adopted Pharaonic practice, establishing themselves as god-kings

entities.name: Ptolemaieia
entities.role: ruler cult festival associated with a temple at Alexandria

entities.name: Peter Green
entities.role: scholar who argued ruler cults did not produce genuine belief in rulers' divinity among Greeks and Macedonians

entities.name: Alexandria
entities.role: great center of Hellenistic culture and capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, where Alexander's tomb was located

entities.name: Antioch
entities.role: great center of Hellenistic culture and capital of Seleucid Syria

entities.name: Cleopatra VII
entities.role: last Ptolemaic queen, known for her role in Roman political battles and whose suicide marked the end of Ptolemaic rule

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.role: Roman figure involved in political battles with Pompey and in relation to Cleopatra VII

entities.name: Mark Antony
entities.role: Roman triumvir defeated at the Battle of Actium along with Cleopatra VII

entities.name: Octavian
entities.role: Roman figure in political battles with Mark Antony; later Augustus, who invaded and took Egypt

entities.name: Battle of Actium
entities.role: battle in 31 BC marking the emergence of the Roman Empire

entities.name: Philip V
entities.role: king of Macedon who allied with Carthage and fought Rome in the Macedonian Wars

entities.name: Battle of Cynoscephalae
entities.role: decisive Roman victory (197 BC) in the Second Macedonian War

entities.name: Perseus
entities.role: son of Philip V whose defeat in the Third Macedonian War ended Antigonid Macedon

entities.name: Achaean League
entities.role: federated league of Greek city-states, the last stronghold of Greek independence, which fought Rome

entities.name: Lucius Mummius
entities.role: Roman consul who defeated the Greeks at Corinth

entities.name: Judas Maccabeus
entities.role: leader of the Maccabean Revolt whose victory is celebrated in Hanukkah

entities.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
entities.role: Seleucid king who sacked Jerusalem and banned Jewish religious rites

entities.name: Euclid
entities.role: mathematician whose works advanced Greek science

entities.name: Archimedes
entities.role: polymath whose works advanced Greek science

entities.name: Zeuxis
entities.role: painter said to have painted grapes so realistic that birds pecked at them

entities.name: Peiraikos
entities.role: artist who chose mundane and lower class subjects for his paintings

entities.name: Aetolian League
entities.role: federated league of Greek city-states that allied with Rome against Macedon

entities.name: Seleucus
entities.role: Seleucid ruler who defeated Antigonus at the Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE)
